source.title: The Eigenlearning Framework: A Conservation Law Perspective on Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
source.authors: James B. Simon; Madeline Dickens; Dhruva Karkada; M. DeWeese

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives its own theoretical account of when double-descent peaks arise in KRR and distinguishes another kind of nonmonotonic sample-size curve from double descent.
record.gate_note: The paper does not sweep model size or report an epoch-wise double-descent curve. Its deep-bootstrap plots and low-sample MSE increases bear on related behavior but do not establish the versions' specified double-descent conditions. Statements attributed to cited work were not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is a theory and experiment paper on kernel ridge regression (KRR) generalization. It reports no double-descent curve along model size, epochs or samples. Its only double-descent content is a one-sentence interpretation in Section 4.2: the overfitting coefficient E0 blows up when kernel eigenvalues drop sharply around index n. That sentence attributes ridge avoidance of peaks to prior work (Canatar et al. 2021; Nakkiran et al. 2021). Section 4.3 studies a low-n increase in MSE that the authors explicitly call distinct from double descent. The deep-bootstrap experiments show no fall-rise-fall shape. No version is tested by the study's own results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors present a learnability conservation law and the eigenlearning equations as a simpler, interpretable KRR generalization theory. They apply it to the deep bootstrap, parity hardness, adversarial smoothness and a free Fermi gas analogy. The double-descent remark is a brief interpretive aside, partly citing prior work, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops theoretical KRR risk equations and tests them on synthetic domains and datasets; it does not reproduce the original model-size double-descent sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that the low-sample MSE increase depends on the target eigenmode and its eigenvalue relative to the spectrum and ridge parameter. Deep-bootstrap curves vary with sample size and effective training time.

fits_no_version.finding: The derived overfitting coefficient E0 = n/(n - ΣLi²) explodes when learnability concentrates in the top n modes, which happens under a sharp eigenvalue drop at index n. Ridge lowers E0. The authors interpret this as the cause of double-descent peaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In KRR, noise amplification E0 diverges when the spectrum drops sharply around n, and ridge damps it (theoretical, no measured peak).

fits_no_version.finding: For modes whose eigenvalue falls below Σλj²/(2(Σλj+δ)), MSE rises with n from n=0, with no initial drop. This matches experiment on three domains (Figure 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-sample MSE can rise immediately with n for hard eigenmodes, a nonmonotonicity distinct from double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Error curves for different n overlap early in training, then peel off. This happens both in ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and in KRR with varying effective training time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep bootstrap is explained by a transition from a regularization-limited regime to a data-limited regime near τeff ≈ 1/κ0.

record.problems: The paper notes that its KRR eigenframework is not experimentally tested at scale on larger structured-kernel settings. The double-descent mechanism is presented as a theoretical interpretation rather than a direct experimental sweep of peaks, and the ridge-avoidance statement points to prior work.
record.rows_left_out: No numerical values were transcribed from figures where the text supplied only plotted curves. Cited results about double-descent peaks and regularization were excluded.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep and no peak at the interpolating size.
No fall-rise-fall test error over training time. The deep-bootstrap curves show no such shape.
No sample-wise increase near the interpolation threshold. The low-n increase is declared a different phenomenon.
No measured second descent past interpolation in any model class. There is only a remark, citing Canatar et al., that double descent needs a sharp spectral cutoff.
No test of a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.

The noise/overfitting mechanism is asserted theoretically via E0 but never shown on a measured peak. Multiple descent and removal of the peak by tuned regularization are not tested; the latter is cited to prior work.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 'supports' label is removed: the study measures no double-descent peak, and the regularization claim is attributed to Canatar et al. (2021) and Nakkiran et al. (2021). The paper is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and a peak near the size that just fits the training set.
Fall-rise-fall test error over training epochs; the deep-bootstrap experiment does not report that shape.
An increase in test error as sample size grows near the interpolation threshold. The paper's reported low-sample increase is explicitly distinguished from double descent.
A general second-descent curve across model classes after interpolation.
A test that one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper's theoretical discussion links double-descent peaks to noise overfitting in KRR; it does not test triple or multiple descent or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Whether counting complexity by effective parameters converts second descent to an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: KRR
rows.operation_detail: Derive and interpret the eigenlearning test-risk and overfitting-coefficient equations.

conditions.value: the discussion identifies a ridge parameter as a hedge against overfitting

rows.measure: Test MSE and pure-noise overfitting coefficient
rows.value: The paper attributes double-descent peaks to noise overfitting when kernel eigenvalues drop sharply around index n; spreading learnability or sacrificing some learnability to ridge lowers E0.
rows.note: This is the paper's theoretical account of the noise/overfitting mechanism, not an experimental sweep demonstrating peak removal by tuned regularization.
rows.check: This is a theoretical interpretation of the E0 equation, not a measured peak. No double-descent curve, peak height or ridge-tuned removal is shown in the study's results. The ridge-removal statement is cited to prior work. It should not be linked to V6 or marked observed.

rows.subject: KRR and trained networks (aggregate across the reported domains)
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of training samples at small n and report test MSE for eigenfunction targets.
rows.measure: Test MSE as sample count increases
rows.baseline: MSE at n=0 is stated as 1 for the normalized eigenfunction case
rows.value: For sufficiently difficult eigenmodes, MSE increases as samples are added at small n; the paper says this is due to overfitting and is distinct from double descent.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 10 error bars are not specified in the main-text description; the experimental methods state that one-standard-deviation error bars are used for experiments.
rows.note: Aggregate result across domains and reported KRR/network experiments; it is not reported as an increase near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: Links are correct. The low-n increase in MSE is explicitly distinguished from double descent, so it does not bear on V3, which concerns behaviour near the interpolation threshold. Figure 10 covers the unit circle, 6d hypercube and 2-sphere, as recorded.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Plot train and test classification error against training steps for different training-set sizes.

conditions.value: data augmentation and SGD; four-run mean

rows.measure: Train and test classification error over training steps
rows.value: The text says the error curves for all n overlap at early times, then train and test error peel off the shared curve at roughly the same time.
rows.uncertainty: The curves are means of 4 training runs; no numerical interval stated.
rows.note: The stated result concerns the deep-bootstrap pattern, not a fall-rise-fall epoch-wise double-descent curve.
rows.check: This is a reproduction of the deep bootstrap (overlapping curves across n). It shows no epoch-wise fall-rise-fall test error, so it is correctly not linked to V2.

rows.subject: KRR with a fully connected four-hidden-layer width-500 network NTK
rows.operation_detail: Vary training-set size and effective training time in KRR on binarized MNIST.
rows.measure: Train and test MSE over effective training time
rows.value: The text says the KRR and ResNet plots share the deep-bootstrap pattern: error curves for all n overlap early, with test and train error peeling off at roughly the same time.
rows.uncertainty: The curves are means of 10 training runs; no numerical interval stated.
rows.note: This tests the deep-bootstrap account, not whether test error follows a fall-rise-fall curve over epochs.
rows.check: This is a KRR proxy for the deep bootstrap over effective training time. It reports no epoch-wise double-descent shape.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical KRR account of noise-related overfitting
reader_labels.reason: The paper's own risk analysis attributes double-descent peaks to noise overfitting under a sharp eigenvalue drop and describes ridge as a hedge (r1).
